records.name: AAV (adeno-associated virus) vector
records.tldr: An AAV vector is a small engineered virus particle used to carry a DNA cassette into cells. Reaching a cell, keeping the DNA and making useful protein are separate steps, and each needs its own evidence in the cells that matter.
records.summary:
Recombinant AAV replaces the viral coding sequence with a designed cassette and regulatory sequences. The protein shell (capsid) influences which cells the particle enters; the cassette decides what those cells could make. The DNA still has to reach the nucleus and act as a template before RNA and protein appear, and an AAV is a different virus from an adenovirus.

Where the DNA sits was measured in different systems. In sequential muscle biopsies taken 3 and 12 months after an intramuscular AAV vector expressing alpha-1 antitrypsin, most vector DNA was double-stranded circular episomes, and clones recovered from the biopsies were transcriptionally active (Schnepp and colleagues; abstract read, full text not retrievable). After partial hepatectomy in mice, extrachromosomal genomes were the main form behind liver expression and in most cases no more than about 10 per cent of stably transduced genomes had integrated, although one of three mice at a higher dose had 67 per cent integrated genomes (Nakai and colleagues). That shows the usual behaviour of the tested vectors in those tissues, not that integration never happens, and persistent DNA does not show an intact cassette, enough protein or a surviving functional cell: in the muscle study the episomal inverted terminal repeats ranged from fully intact to severely deleted, so counting vector DNA is a different measurement from showing a working cassette.

Immunity and capacity also limit what a lot can do. In a phase 1/2 study in seven people with severe haemophilia B, an AAV2 factor IX vector infused through the hepatic artery reached therapeutic levels at the highest dose but expression lasted about 8 weeks; the authors' further studies suggested that cell-mediated immunity against capsid antigens destroyed transduced hepatocytes (Manno and colleagues). Neutralising antibodies against the capsid are why re-dosing is hard: a review notes that systemic AAV dosing needs patient stratification by antibody level and that re-administration then becomes very difficult (Naso and colleagues), and a 2024 mouse study, which opens by noting that AAV typically induces long-lasting neutralising antibodies that prevent re-administration, found that transient B-cell depletion (anti-CD20 with anti-BAFF) before hepatic AAV8 delivery allowed effective re-administration (Rana and colleagues). Whether a given product can be given again is a product-specific question, and that mouse experiment does not establish a clinical re-dosing protocol. For packaging, the AAV2 genome is a single-stranded DNA of 4,675 nucleotides (Srivastava and colleagues) and the original self-complementary-vector experiment used an inverted repeat that could pair with itself, bypassing synthesis of the second strand (McCarty and colleagues, 2001). McCarty's later review describes the trade-off as losing half the coding capacity. Report the capsid, cassette configuration and length being measured with a capacity figure; a measured packaged-genome length and usable coding capacity answer different questions. In the study of plasmid-encoded vectors of 4.7 to 8.7 kb in AAV2, AAV5 and AAV8 capsids, packaged genomes never exceeded 5.2 kb; genomes from plasmids over 5 kb were heterogeneous and truncated at the 5' end, and reporter expression in cells at high multiplicity of infection was substantially lower than from genomes under 5 kb (Wu and colleagues). FDA follow-up guidance says vectors such as AAV that do not tend to integrate or reactivate generally carry a lower risk of delayed adverse events, while product-specific modifications may change that, so safety is assessed per product.

AAV also appears in cell-engineering workflows without being the lasting product. In primary human T cells in culture, Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA were electroporated and a recombinant AAV6 vector added 2 to 4 hours later supplied a repair template encoding a CD19 CAR, which was knocked into the TRAC locus; the edited cells outperformed conventionally generated CAR T cells in a mouse leukaemia model (Eyquem and colleagues). There the AAV carried a donor template into cells outside the body and the lasting change was the knocked-in receptor, so an AAV in a workflow does not show direct targeting of T cells in a patient. Capsid variants differ in tissue tropism, for example AAV8 for liver in rodents and non-human primates (Naso and colleagues).

Muscle and liver observations, T-cell editing in culture and mouse leukaemia experiments answer different questions. Muscle or liver persistence does not establish how another cassette behaves in dividing T cells. A capsid that favours a tissue is a delivery feature, separate from what the encoded protein recognises; the cited experiments do not establish benefit for people with cancer.

records.name: Targeted lipid nanoparticles
records.tldr: Targeted lipid nanoparticles use a surface ligand or a changed lipid mix to favour particular cells or organs. Enrichment in a tissue is not the same as working protein made only in the intended cell type.
records.summary:
Two strategies are separate. A ligand strategy adds a binding molecule such as an antibody to the particle surface so it recognises a marker on intended cells; binding must still lead to uptake and usable release, and the marker may sit on other cells. A formulation strategy changes the lipids: selective organ targeting (SORT) added a supplemental lipid to otherwise standard LNPs and, after intravenous injection in mice, shifted delivery toward lung, spleen or liver; with a Cre reporter, the lung formulation edited about 40 per cent of epithelial and 65 per cent of endothelial cells, the spleen formulation 12 per cent of B cells and 10 per cent of T cells, and the liver formulation 93 per cent of hepatocytes (Cheng and colleagues, as reported). These are measured results in mice, not a rule connecting a composition to an organ in people.

A CD5-directed example shows both the aim and its limit. CD5-targeted LNPs carrying modified mRNA for a chimeric antigen receptor against fibroblast activation protein were tested in activated mouse T cells in culture (81 per cent expressed a GFP reporter and 83 per cent the receptor, against 7 per cent with isotype-control antibody particles) and then injected intravenously into mice with angiotensin II and phenylephrine induced cardiac injury. Receptor expression appeared in each major T-cell subset by flow cytometry (87 per cent of receptor-positive T cells were CD4-positive), bioluminescence showed spleen targeting only with CD5 particles, and liver expression occurred with both CD5 and control particles, so an organ-level signal and the identity of the expressing cells were measured separately; treatment reduced fibrosis and restored cardiac function in these mice (Rurik and colleagues, author manuscript). The delivery address was CD5 and the encoded receptor recognised a different target. This was a fibrosis model, not a cancer trial, and the authors disclose patents on the platforms.

A later study used targeted LNPs to deliver mRNA to specific T-cell subsets; its abstract reports reprogrammed CD8-positive T cells in samples from healthy donors and people with autoimmune disease, tumour control in humanised mice and B-cell depletion in cynomolgus monkeys (Hunter and colleagues; abstract only, full text not retrievable). Each of those is a different experiment in a different setting, and none is evidence of benefit against solid tumours in people.

Enrichment is not exclusivity. In a Cre-reporter experiment recombination appeared in 81.1 per cent of CD4-positive and 75.6 per cent of CD8-positive splenocytes but also in 15.0 per cent of CD3-negative cells, mainly B cells, dendritic cells and macrophages (Rurik and colleagues), and the 87 per cent figure above is a share of receptor-positive cells, not the share of CD4 T cells that expressed the receptor, so the denominator matters. Cargo type also matters for how long the effect lasts: RNA encoding a receptor produced transient CAR T cells in that study, whereas RNA encoding a genome editor can leave a lasting DNA change, as when SORT lipid nanoparticles delivered Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA to edit cells in mice (Cheng and colleagues) and Cas9 mRNA with an AAV repair template knocked a CAR into T cells in culture (Eyquem and colleagues).

Organ signal, cell identity, protein function and clinical effect need separate measurements, with matched untargeted controls and identified intended and unintended recipient populations.

records.name: Cell-therapy release and potency testing
records.tldr: A cell-product lot is checked against specified quality requirements before its disposition. Identity, live-cell measures and biological activity answer different questions about that lot.
records.summary: FDA's final potency-assurance guidance describes a product-specific strategy spanning manufacturing design, controls, materials, in-process testing and lot-release assays. CAR T-cell guidance separately discusses safety, identity, quality, purity and potency measurements. A viability result or marker-expression result is not automatically equivalent to a functional bioassay. Assay choice and acceptance criteria depend on the product and development context. Passing a release specification is distinct from estimating clinical benefit in a patient.

notes: FDA's November 2026 final potency-assurance guidance supersedes its January 2011 potency-tests guidance. Its scope is cellular and gene therapy biological products regulated under section 351 of the U.S. Public Health Service Act. Potency assurance includes process and material controls, in-process evidence, release assays, stability and in-use handling; a release assay alone does not establish the clinical benefit of a particular lot. Federal Register notice 2026-22427, published 3 November 2026, announces the final guidance and finalises the December 2023 draft.

For CAR T cells, FDA's 2024 guidance recommends identity evidence for the transgene and intended cellular composition. HLA typing alone does not detect the genetic modification or replace chain-of-identity records. Biological identity and the association with the intended recipient are separate checks.

For an integrating-vector CAR T-cell product, the 2024 guidance describes average vector copy number per CAR-positive cell on the lot certificate of analysis. Including CAR-negative cells in the denominator can understate the value in the modified population. The average does not show insertion locations or clonal distribution. Short processes can retain non-integrated vector copies, so a release measurement may need a later assessment in cultured cells to determine stable integration; the interval is product-specific.

Replication-competent virus testing, microbial sterility, mycoplasma, endotoxin and engineered-cell identity address different hazards or attributes. The applicable tests, methods and acceptance criteria depend on the product, process and development stage. Detecting a sequence or a receptor does not demonstrate every intended biological activity.

For ex vivo genetically modified cells administered immediately after manufacture, FDA's 2020 gene-therapy CMC guidance describes an in-process sterility sample taken 48 to 72 hours before final harvest plus a rapid test such as a Gram stain on final product. Under that approach, negative Gram stain and no growth in the in-process test can support release while the final-product culture continues for its full duration, for example 14 days for USP <71>. The guidance calls for a plan addressing a later positive result, clinical management, investigation and reporting to the investigator and FDA. These are scoped recommendations, not universal early-release criteria for every cell product.

FDA's CAR T-cell examples distinguish activity against each target in a multi-antigen product, production of an added cytokine and a drug-resistance function. Each relevant transgene activity may need suitable evidence. A single expression or cell-count result is not the complete functional package.

In a fictional 100-cell teaching sample, 80 cells are live and 60 of those live cells express the receptor. Viability is 80/100, receptor positivity among live cells is 60/80, and live receptor-positive cells among all counted cells are 60/100. Receptor status of the nonlive cells is unspecified. These different denominators establish neither potency nor a clinical release cutoff.

Scope boundary with general release records. This record owns release and potency testing of cell and gene products. General lot disposition, out-of-specification handling and good manufacturing practice are taught in the batch release and good manufacturing practice records; decaying radiopharmaceuticals are in radiopharmaceutical quality and release.

Potency is relevant biological activity under defined conditions. FDA's November 2026 guidance aims for every released lot to have the ability to achieve the intended therapeutic effect and expects the relationship between a measured attribute and the product's mechanism of action to be supported by characterisation, nonclinical or clinical studies; where the mechanism is not fully understood, a statistical relationship such as a correlation with outcomes may help. Identity, receptor expression and viability do not establish activity.

Direct and surrogate measures. A direct biological assay measures activity such as target-cell killing; a surrogate measures a related attribute and needs a supported link to function. FDA's January 2011 potency guidance (now superseded) used the term assay matrix for complementary tests. The 2026 guidance recommends developing multiple assays that measure potency-related CQAs early, with redundant assays discontinued later. Many unrelated measurements do not add up to potency.

Controls, reference material and handling state. Potency protocols should set predefined sample and system suitability criteria, and a run should be invalidated if system suitability fails. Reference material lots should be qualified and monitored for stability. Release assays must use a sample taken after all manufacturing steps that may affect potency, with cryopreservation named as an example, so a test on fresh material does not stand for the final product.

Reading a killing result. A figure such as 60 per cent killing is not comparable between laboratories unless target identity, effector-to-target ratio and observation time are stated, and relative potency needs a named reference and model. FDA's CAR T guidance describes orthogonal methods such as a cell-killing assay, transduction efficiency and cytokine measurement. No universal passing cutoff applies across products.

Validation is about the assay, not the drug. The 2026 guidance asks that release assays measure potency with sufficient specificity, accuracy or precision over their reportable range, that performance be established under actual conditions of use, and that phase-appropriate acceptance criteria be set with failing lots rejected. Qualification and validation do not show that a drug improves a clinical endpoint.

Different questions. Sterility and potency are separate attributes with separate tests, and a passing potency result is a quality finding, not a clinical response rate. Inference lesson: a lot with high viability and receptor expression whose target-specific killing falls below its predefined criterion is not rescued by the two passing tests, and the failure is investigated under the controlled process.

records.name: Cell-product chain of identity and custody
records.tldr: Identity records connect cells and products to their source and intended recipient. Custody records show who held them and what happened during handoffs.
records.summary: Traceability preserves relationships across source material, engineering construct, processing lots, containers, samples and intended recipients. Chain of identity and chain of custody answer different questions: what material and recipient are associated, and who had responsibility at each stage under which recorded conditions. A coded identifier makes a relationship recordable; it does not independently prove that the label, material and recipient agree.

notes: A collection can branch into processing lots, doses or test samples. Retain parent links and construct versions so a sample result can be attributed to the material it represents. One bag need not mean one manufacturing run or one dose; an allogeneic workflow can relate donor material to later recipients according to its actual design.

ICCBBA ST-028 version 1.1.0, June 2025, describes chain-of-identity relationships and responsibilities. IG-050 version 1.0.0, December 2023, gives bounded examples in which material is returned to the same patient; it explicitly does not cover one collection manufactured into therapies for multiple patients. That example scope must not be generalised into a complete donor-bank scheme.

In a fictional single-recipient example, collection A produces lot A, which branches into doses A1 and A2 and test sample S. Each child retains the parent link. A separate custody trail records handlers, handoff times and conditions. Keeping those links does not establish acceptable quality or clinical suitability.

Barcodes, biological identity assays, HLA typing, potency results and temperature traces are different evidence. None alone replaces the complete material/intended-recipient verification. A discrepancy or excursion requires investigation and the authorised quality disposition; an audit trail is evidence to assess, not a guarantee of safety.

FDA's CAR T-cell guidance addresses documented tracking from collection to administration and independent recipient/label checks. The required process is not equivalent to purchasing a particular orchestration system. Research samples, fresh products, cryopreserved products and in vivo carriers retain their own applicable identities and handling context.

records.name: Cryopreservation and cell-therapy cold chain
records.tldr: Freezing, storage, shipping and thawing can preserve cells for later use. The validated conditions and checks belong to the particular cell product.
records.summary: Cryopreservation manages cooling, water movement, ice formation, concentrated solutes and warming injury; it does not literally stop all molecular motion. Cryoprotectant formulation, exposure, freezing, storage, transport, thawing and permitted holding times form a defined process. Some materials are handled fresh. A temperature log documents conditions, while stability evidence and the quality system determine the consequences of a deviation. Neither a shipper nor a barcode guarantees viable, functional material or the correct recipient.

records.name: Good manufacturing practice (GMP)
records.tldr: Good manufacturing practice is the set of controls over people, materials, equipment, procedures and records that is meant to make each batch of a medicine consistently as it should be. It is a property of how a product is made, not a finding about whether the treatment works.
records.summary: The US Food and Drug Administration describes current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) as systems that assure proper design, monitoring and control of manufacturing processes and facilities, including quality management systems, suitable raw materials, written operating procedures, detection and investigation of deviations, and reliable testing laboratories; the 'C' stands for current, meaning technologies and systems must be up to date. FDA's quality-systems guidance gives a quality unit the job of reviewing procedures, evidence and departures from the intended process. Requirements depend on stage: most phase 1 investigational drugs are exempt from 21 CFR part 211 under 21 CFR 210.2(c), but FDA's 2008 phase 1 guidance applies CGMP under section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to them, so 'investigational' does not mean quality controls are optional. A passing final test does not close the process question: an unexplained substitution or missing record needs its own documented assessment. GMP concerns how a product is made; the product dossier (chemistry, manufacturing and controls), the decision on one lot (batch release) and clinical evidence answer different questions.

GMP combines people, procedures, materials, equipment and records into a working quality system. FDA's CGMP page says it covers quality management systems, quality raw materials, written operating procedures, detection and investigation of deviations and reliable testing laboratories, and that the C stands for current, requiring technologies and systems that are up to date. A clean room is one part of the system and not proof of compliance by itself.

In-process controls and the final sample. FDA's quality-systems guidance describes quality control as assessing incoming components, in-process materials and finished product and evaluating how the manufacturing process performs. A final sample answers a narrower question about tested material and cannot reconstruct an unrecorded process, so a passing final test does not close the question raised by, for example, an unexplained material substitution.

The quality unit approves or rejects incoming materials, in-process materials and drug products, reviews production records and investigates unexplained discrepancies. Investigating a deviation asks what happened, which material may be affected and how to prevent recurrence; a missing record and a failed test are different findings that both need an explanation.

Changes need control, because replacing a supplier or a processing step may alter the product. Q5E-style comparability asks whether relevant quality remains comparable; it does not assume that a familiar product name means unchanged biology.

GMP supports reliable clinical investigation; it does not show efficacy.

records.name: Lentiviral vector
records.tldr: A lentiviral vector is an engineered virus particle that delivers genetic instructions into cells, and in most designs those instructions are inserted into a chromosome. Getting in, being inserted, making protein and doing the intended job are four separate claims.
records.summary:
Common lentiviral vectors package an RNA genome. After entry the RNA is reverse-transcribed into DNA, and in an integrating design the enzyme integrase helps insert that DNA into the cell's chromosomes, where an internal promoter can drive the encoded protein. The envelope proteins influence which cells the particle enters; changing the envelope changes delivery, not what an encoded receptor recognises.

Three design labels are easy to confuse. Replication-defective means the delivered particle lacks the machinery to propagate as an ordinary virus, which does not replace testing: FDA guidance sets out testing of retroviral vector products, lentiviral ones included, for replication-competent virus during manufacture and in patient follow-up. Self-inactivating means regulatory sequences in the long terminal repeats are disabled: in the original design a 133 base-pair deletion in the U3 region of the 3' repeat was copied to the 5' repeat after reverse transcription and integration, and the vector still expressed from an internal promoter in rat brain and eye (Miyoshi and colleagues). It does not mean the cassette cannot integrate. Integration-deficient means integrase is mutated: with a class 1 integrase mutation, residual integration was lower than with intact integrase by a factor of 500 to 1,250, expression was transient in dividing cell lines and long-lived in non-dividing neural cultures and in mouse brain, consistent with an episomal genome (Philippe and colleagues). The name does not promise zero integration or lasting expression in dividing cells such as T cells.

The foundational HIV-based design transduced HeLa cells and rat fibroblasts blocked in the cell cycle and primary human macrophages, and gave stable gene transfer into terminally differentiated neurons in vivo (Naldini and colleagues; abstract read). FDA follow-up guidance notes that the activity of retroviral vectors, lentiviral ones included, comes from an integration event that is generally not directed to specific genomic sites, which raises the possibility of disrupting important genes; the risk depends on the whole product and cells.

In clinical use, third-generation self-inactivating vectors disrupt the promoter and enhancer activity of the long terminal repeat, non-integrating vectors lacking integrase have been investigated to avoid insertional mutagenesis, and recombination during manufacture could in theory produce replication-competent retrovirus or lentivirus, which is why lots are tested (Milone and O'Doherty, review).

Measurement keeps layers apart. For CAR T products FDA recommends testing vector lots for transducing units per millilitre in a suitable cell line or healthy donor cells, and reporting vector copy number, the average number of integrations per CAR-positive cell; dividing by all cells, including CAR-negative ones, lowers the reported figure, so the denominator has to be stated (FDA, January 2024). Particle or genome counts, a functional titre, copies per cell, receptor-positive percentage and antigen-dependent activity answer different questions, a particle can be counted yet not transduce, and an average copy number does not show each cell's copy number or insertion sites. These are laboratory, animal and regulatory sources, not evidence of benefit in cancer.

records.name: Insertional mutagenesis
records.tldr: Insertional mutagenesis is a change in a cell's genes caused by added genetic material landing in its DNA and disrupting a gene or its control, and neither an insertion nor a growing cell clone shows by itself that a cancer has formed or what caused it.
records.summary:
Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

Three primary reports show why the setting matters. After retrovirus-mediated gamma-c gene transfer into autologous CD34-positive bone marrow cells for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, 9 of 10 patients were corrected, but almost three years later the two youngest developed uncontrolled clonal proliferation of mature T cells; both clones carried vector integration near the LMO2 proto-oncogene promoter with abnormal LMO2 expression, which the authors attributed most likely to retrovirus enhancer activity (Hacein-Bey-Abina et al., 2003). In a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia given CD19 CAR T cells, 94 per cent of CAR T cells at the peak of response came from one clone in which lentiviral insertion had disrupted TET2, the patient's second TET2 allele carried a hypomorphic mutation, and the clone showed a central memory phenotype alongside complete remission: an expanded clone linked to benefit, not a new cancer (Fraietta et al., 2018). In 724 patients treated with T-cell therapies at one centre, a lethal T-cell lymphoma followed axicabtagene ciloleucel for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; the tumour, the CAR T cells and the patient's normal blood cells were profiled in depth, both lymphomas were Epstein-Barr virus positive and linked to DNMT3A and TET2 mutant clonal haematopoiesis, and no evidence of oncogenic retroviral integration was found with multiple techniques (Hamilton et al., 2024). The first is a specific stem-cell regimen and the others are single-centre or single-patient observations, so none is an incidence estimate for a vector or product.

What regulators ask for follows from this. The August 2026 ABECMA prescribing information carries a boxed warning that T-cell malignancies, including CAR-positive tumours, have occurred after BCMA- and CD19-directed genetically modified autologous T-cell immunotherapies for blood cancers, may present within weeks of infusion and may be fatal, and says to monitor life-long for secondary malignancies. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance recommends following people for 15 years after treatment with CAR T cells containing an integrated transgene, because integrating vectors may increase the risk of delayed adverse events and non-integrating vectors are thought to carry a low delayed risk. These are class-level product warnings and follow-up expectations; they do not assign one mechanism to every event or give an incidence for other products.

To attribute a malignancy after engineered-cell therapy, investigators ask whether the therapeutic sequence is present in the malignant cells, where the integrations are, whether they alter relevant genes, whether related clones were detectable earlier, and what prior therapy, underlying disease and pre-existing genetic changes contribute. Integration-site sequencing maps insertion locations, quantitative DNA assays estimate vector copies per cell, and flow cytometry, gene-expression measurement and pathology answer different questions about identity, function and malignancy; the sample is consumed by testing. Average vector copy number cannot show the position or effect of each insertion, a clone's frequency depends on the sampled cells, assay sensitivity and time, and blood may not represent every tissue. This record gives no copy-number or clone-frequency threshold because none of the sources read sets one. Messenger RNA delivery that does not integrate does not use genomic insertion as its route, which does not remove its other risks.

records.name: Transposon systems for cell engineering
records.tldr: An engineered DNA transposon is a gene-insertion system in which an enzyme, the transposase, places a designed cassette into a cell's DNA. A separate method has to deliver the pieces first, and non-viral does not mean non-integrating.
records.summary:
A transposon system has two parts: a cargo cassette flanked by boundary sequences, and a transposase that recognises those boundaries and catalyses insertion. The transposase can be supplied as protein or through instructions that make it, and the cell has to receive both in usable form; the system does not itself deliver anything. Sleeping Beauty was reconstructed from inactive fish elements, and its transposase bound the inverted repeats and mediated precise cut-and-paste transposition in fish, mouse and human cells (Ivics and colleagues).

In one reported clinical example, two phase I trials in 26 people (7 autologous, 19 allogeneic) electroporated peripheral blood mononuclear cells with Sleeping Beauty transposon and transposase plasmids encoding a CD19-specific CAR and expanded them on activating and propagating cells for a median of 28 days. The abstract reports 2,200 to 2,500-fold ex vivo expansion, 84 per cent CAR expression, no integration hotspots, no acute or late toxicities reported, and CAR T-cell persistence averaging 201 days in autologous and 51 days in allogeneic recipients; the discussion states that the products were free of detectable SB11 transposase (Kebriaei and colleagues). That is a feasibility and safety report in small uncontrolled trials, and it describes cells engineered outside the body, not injected components.

Systems differ. In primary human T cells from peripheral blood and cord blood, piggyBac gave the highest stable gene transfer efficiency in the peripheral-blood cells and the most integrants in both, Tol2 and piggyBac were more likely to promote clonal expansion than Sleeping Beauty, and Tol2 and piggyBac integrated near transcription start sites and CpG islands while Sleeping Beauty integrations looked random (Huang and colleagues). That is a laboratory comparison, not a ranking of safety in patients. Insertion-site sequencing recovers only some junctions: in the Sleeping Beauty trial's 33 independent libraries most shared fewer than 20 per cent of sites with any other library, which the authors read as arguing against common hotspots, although some pairs shared over 40 per cent and 100,000 of 571,533 unique integrations were mapped. That describes those libraries, not every insertion or later clone, and an average copy number hides differences between cells. FDA follow-up guidance states that integration by transposon elements is not directed to specific sites and that continuing transposase in target cells creates the potential for remobilising an inserted element, so transposase persistence and cassette persistence are separate measurements.

records.name: RNA-lipoplex
records.tldr: An RNA-lipoplex is a particle in which RNA is complexed with lipids. Its behaviour depends on the exact lipids, charge balance and route, so a result for one lipoplex does not transfer to another product.
records.summary:
RNA carries negative charge, and positively charged lipid components can associate with it. RNA-lipoplex names a family of formulations, and the final particle need not be positively charged: net charge depends on the balance of RNA and lipid, the ingredients and the preparation. The naming overlaps with lipid nanoparticles, so the actual composition and properties matter more than the acronym.

In one study of the approach, intravenous RNA-lipoplexes were aimed at dendritic cells by adjusting net charge, without adding a molecular ligand; the particles protected RNA from ribonucleases, were taken up and expressed in dendritic cells and macrophages in lymphoid compartments, and triggered interferon-alpha release from plasmacytoid dendritic cells and macrophages, with antigen-specific T-cell responses and tumour rejection in the authors' in vivo experiments (Kranz and colleagues; the abstract also reports a phase I trial in which three people with melanoma had been treated at a low dose when it was published). An innate-immune signal is not antigen expression, antigen-specific immunity or clinical benefit.

The pancreatic cancer vaccine autogene cevumeran shows how specific a lipoplex product is. In the phase I trial each patient's vaccine held two uridine mRNA strands, each encoding up to 10 neoepitopes, formulated in lipoplex nanoparticles of about 400 nm made from the cationic lipid DOTMA and the phospholipid DOPE, given intravenously (Rojas and colleagues, methods). That trial gave atezolizumab and the vaccine to 16 people and then a modified FOLFIRINOX regimen to 15, so it describes one product within a treatment sequence and neither ranks lipoplexes against lipid nanoparticles nor isolates the vaccine's effect.

A commercial cationic-lipid lipoplex reagent shows how far charge and properties can vary. In vitro, eGFP mRNA lipoplexes formed in pure water measured 98.7 to 121.5 nm by dynamic light scattering and had zeta potentials from -14.4 to -58.7 mV across reagent lots, so a cationic lipid does not guarantee a positive particle, and the value was measured for that preparation, medium and lot (Appelbaum and colleagues; canine retina and cell lines, no cancer setting). The same study separates uptake from expression: after subretinal injection eGFP mRNA was detected in all retinal cell types but protein was limited to the retinal pigment epithelium. A product with the same antigen sequence but different lipids or route is not the same product: particle size and route changed where mRNA LNPs went in mice (Di and colleagues), and the Rojas product is described by its own composition, route and protocol.

For messenger RNA, being inside an endosome is not enough: it must reach the cytosol to be translated. The endosomal-release experiments summarised under lipid nanoparticles used LNPs, not lipoplexes, so they do not by themselves describe a lipoplex.

records.name: Synthetic cytokine receptors
records.tldr: An engineered cytokine receptor connects a specified input to signalling inside a cell. The added signal and the behaviour of the complete cell product need separate measurements.
records.summary: A synthetic cytokine receptor is an engineered cell-surface protein that connects a specified input to intracellular signalling. It differs from engineering a soluble cytokine or simply administering a cytokine. Some designs require an externally supplied ligand; others generate ligand-independent signalling. The receptor domains, input, expression and cell type define the tested construct. A growth-supporting signal does not itself establish antigen recognition, entry into a tumour, completed killing or durable patient benefit.

records.name: JAK-STAT signalling
records.tldr: The relay that turns cytokine signals into gene changes. Overactive in blood cancers (JAK2 in myelofibrosis), it is also the wire that carries interferon's cancer-killing message, so tumours cut it to escape immunotherapy.
records.summary: Cytokine receptors recruit JAK kinases that phosphorylate STAT transcription factors. JAK2 V617F drives myeloproliferative neoplasms (ruxolitinib, fedratinib, momelotinib approved); STAT3 is a hub for IL-6-driven survival, immunosuppression, and cachexia; STAT5 in leukaemias. Interferon-γ signalling via JAK1/2-STAT1 upregulates MHC and PD-L1; JAK1/2 loss-of-function mutations cause acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade. Direct STAT3 inhibitors (degraders, antisense) are in early trials.

records.name: Cytokine
records.tldr: Small proteins immune cells use to talk to each other: alarms, recruitment calls, growth orders and stand-down signals. Some are cancer drugs, and a flood of them is the danger of certain immunotherapies.
records.summary: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

records.tldr: Cytokine therapy supplies immune-signalling proteins or cells that produce them. Effects depend on the molecule, receiving cells and exposure, with benefits and harms specific to the regimen.
records.summary: High-dose IL-2 and interferon-alpha are historic. Engineered IL-2 (bempegaldesleukin failed), IL-15 superagonists (nogapendekin alfa/Anktiva, approved 2024 with BCG in bladder cancer), IL-12 (tavokinogene, intratumoural), and tumour-targeted immunocytokines are the modern forms. IL-2 remains part of TIL therapy regimens.

notes: A cytokine is a signalling protein, and cytokine treatment supplies the protein or causes cells to produce it. The response depends on the molecule, the receiving receptor system, the cell's previous state and its exposure. A neighbourhood-message analogy is useful only to this extent: receiving a signal does not give a cell the correct cancer target or a literal instruction to fight it. IL-2 can influence lymphocyte growth and activity; interferons have different receptors and effects, so one cytokine name cannot stand for every immune signal.

IL-2 can support regulatory T cells as well as other responding lymphocytes. Boyman and colleagues showed in mice that different IL-2-antibody complexes preferentially expanded different T-cell populations, including CD8 cells or CD4 regulatory T cells. The formulation changed the biological effect. Receptor composition, sensitivity and cell state therefore matter when studying a cytokine design; these mouse experiments do not establish human cancer benefit from every complex or from a larger dose.

Circulating protein, local formulations and engineered cytokine-producing cells are different exposure strategies. A local origin does not guarantee local confinement: the signal can reach the circulation and persist elsewhere. In Zhang's 2015 dose-escalation study, 33 people with metastatic melanoma received transferred tumour-infiltrating cells engineered with inducible IL-12. Higher cell doses were associated with high serum IL-12 and interferon gamma and serious liver, fever and circulatory toxicities. The finding concerns that construct and regimen; it does not establish the safety or harm of every armoured cell product.

The U.S. Proleukin prescribing information specifies aldesleukin for adults with metastatic renal cell carcinoma or metastatic melanoma. Its boxed warning includes potentially fatal capillary leak and requires administration in a hospital with an intensive-care facility. These are medicine-specific indications and precautions, not an indication or toxicity rate for all cytokines. Mechanistic plausibility or a diagnosis alone does not select a cytokine regimen.

Haematopoietic growth factors support blood-cell production. For example, G-CSF used to reduce infection risk from low white-cell counts during cancer treatment is supportive care; that use does not by itself establish direct cancer killing. Endogenous cytokine biology, measuring a signal and administering a therapy are different activities. More activation is not automatically more useful immunity, and secretion by an engineered cell is not proof of confined exposure.

A fictional spatial comparison has two equal-sized compartments with cytokine concentrations of 0 and 20 picograms per millilitre, while another has 10 and 10. Both means are 10, but the spatial patterns differ. A whole-sample mean cannot establish directed chemotaxis, which concerns movement in relation to a chemical pattern, an appropriate receiver and a route the cell can traverse. This simplified drawing neither measures migration nor states a requirement for every kind of cell movement.

Measure exposure, receptor signalling, absolute cell number, cell state, functional activity and tumour outcomes separately. A larger sampled cell population can reflect more division, less loss or redistribution into the sampled compartment. A blood count does not by itself describe the tumour. Likewise, a high cytokine concentration or inflammation does not establish efficacy: persistence of useful activity and adverse effects need their own measurements.

For a cytokine design, follow the molecule, formulation and route to tissue exposure, receptor and cell state, useful and unwanted responses, and then clinical outcomes and harms. This is a set of conditional questions. Antigen material, a recognition receptor and cytokine support perform different jobs: adding cytokine-producing armouring does not itself supply cancer specificity or a route into the tumour. The actual combination and disease setting need evidence.

Suppose a fictional cytokine study reports more circulating T cells after treatment but no measurement of their targets or tumour recognition. The count changed, but the result does not identify which populations changed, whether division, survival or redistribution caused it, or whether those cells can recognise and affect the cancer. Functional testing, clinical outcomes, durability and safety remain separate questions.

records.name: Armoured, logic-gated & next-gen CARs
aka: T cells redirected for universal cytokine-mediated killing
records.tldr: Armored immune cells add a specified function, such as cytokine support or a changed response to an inhibitory signal. Each added function brings its own activity and safety questions.
records.summary: Armoring adds functions beyond a basic recognition receptor. Designs include continuous, activation-induced or surface-held cytokine support and modifications to particular inhibitory responses. A dominant-negative TGF-beta receptor is a receptor variant that interferes with signaling; it is different from deleting a receptor gene. Recognition logic and cell-elimination switches are separate design choices. None guarantees access to every tumor, coverage of antigen-negative cells or protection of healthy tissue.

NFAT can also respond to physiological T-cell receptor stimulation, so activation-responsive is not automatically CAR-exclusive or tumor-exclusive. Narayan tested a PSMA CAR with a dominant-negative TGF-beta receptor in a prostate-cancer phase 1 study; a fatal event occurred with severe cytokine release syndrome and concurrent sepsis. Resistance to one signal was not resistance to every inhibitory pathway or every harm.

Inducible production does not establish confinement. In a separate melanoma study, NFAT-driven IL-12-producing TILs were associated with high serum cytokines and serious systemic toxicity. Those cells were TILs, not the same CAR construct as the earlier TRUCK model.

Cytokine concentration, viable-cell abundance and killing at a specified time answer different questions. Greater expansion alone does not establish a wider safety window.

records.name: Tumour microenvironment (TME)
records.tldr: A tumour’s surroundings include cells, vessels, matrix and local conditions. Their presence or location alone does not establish how they affect the cancer or its treatment.
records.summary: Cancer cells interact with neighbouring immune and stromal cells, vessels, extracellular material and physical conditions. These interactions vary across sites, regions and time and can have different consequences. Composition, position, molecular programs and demonstrated function are separate layers of evidence.

The tumour microenvironment includes neighbouring cells, extracellular material, vessels and local physical conditions. A neighbouring cell need not belong to the malignant clone. Cell populations, cytokines and chemokines, matrix, oxygen, nutrients and waste interact in both directions, and their arrangement varies between regions, disease sites and times. A drawing is a map of possible participants, not a measured recipe or a fixed job description.

Keren used multiplexed protein imaging in 41 human triple-negative breast cancers to describe composition and spatial organisation. This is observational evidence. Salmon used viable human lung-tumour slices to investigate matrix and T-cell movement, including a perturbation. The two designs answer different questions, and neither makes stromal removal a universal treatment instruction. Presence or proximity alone does not demonstrate signalling, recognition, killing or suppression.

Retain site, date, treatment, region and denominator: cells per area differs from a fraction of detected cells. Selected-protein imaging, spatial RNA capture with cell assignment and a controlled functional experiment are different outputs. Segmentation can misassign boundaries and dissociation changes which cells are recovered. There is no universal TME score that establishes treatment benefit.

In a fictional macrophage-rich region with inflammatory RNA, composition and expression are observed. The result does not identify every RNA signal’s cellular source, demonstrate macrophage suppression or select the best treatment. A workflow through cells, locations, vessels, matrix and conditions orders questions; it is not a causal chain from cell counts to immune function.

records.name: T-cell states
records.tldr: Response history and measured function help describe a T cell's state. One marker cannot provide a complete label.
records.summary:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

Effector denotes developed response functions, including help or killing; memory can support renewed responses but promises neither permanent protection nor cancer specificity. State categories are not one mandatory developmental trajectory. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression and regulatory role remain distinct.

The same paired receptor can occur with different functional phenotypes and response histories. Fictional R1 memory-associated and progenitor-like exhausted observations are separate observations, not a measured transition. Progenitor-like exhaustion is distinct from ordinary memory; shared TCF1 or division does not make their programmes equivalent.

Fictional equal-looking PD-1-positive populations near cancer have different controlled peptide responses: one viral and one tumour-peptide directed. Marker and proximity do not establish specificity; peptide response does not establish natural tumour display, access or killing. Checkpoint blockade does not rewrite receptor specificity. Preserve tissue, sampling time, population definitions and controlled function alongside RNA/protein panels; favourable markers or division alone cannot predict benefit.

In Burger and colleagues' engineered mouse lung tumours, the subdominant response contained heterogeneous TCF1-positive populations, including a CCR6/Tc17-associated subset that did not preferentially benefit from checkpoint blockade. Long-peptide vaccination with the two model antigens and cyclic di-GMP improved the subdominant response; a subdominant-only arm also tested antigen-specific effects. The separate human analyses were associations, not a validated universal TCF1/CCR6 requirement, target-deletion rule or clone-pruning instruction.

records.name: T-cell exhaustion and CAR-T persistence
records.tldr: T-cell exhaustion describes altered differentiation and function under persistent stimulation. A marker, cell count or persisting CAR transgene does not by itself establish useful tumour killing.
records.summary:
Persistent stimulation can produce heterogeneous T-cell states, rather than one uniformly inactive population. In the studied tumour models, TCF1-positive, PD-1-positive cells could proliferate and generate more differentiated cells during checkpoint treatment. That result does not mean every exhausted cell has been reset. State-associated markers, receptor identity, proliferation and completed target-cell killing answer different questions.

For CAR-T, distinguish the infused preparation, expansion, later detection in blood, viable functional cells at relevant sites and disease control. A 24-patient axi-cel infusion-product study associated memory/exhaustion-related transcriptional features with outcomes; an association in that cohort does not prove that one modification will correct every failure. A detectable transgene is not itself a functional killing assay.

B-cell aplasia is used as a surrogate of CD19-directed activity against normal B cells, not a guarantee that all cancer sites remain controlled. Relapse can occur while aplasia continues. In the 2025 tisagenlecleucel analysis, relationships differed between B-ALL and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; blood transgene levels lacked robust relapse-prediction performance. Early B-cell recovery in B-ALL was also affected by subsequent transplantation and censoring. No universal recovery cutoff or rule that persistence is irrelevant in ALL follows from an early response.

records.name: Adenosine and IDO: two separate routes that can restrain immune responses
records.tldr: Adenosine can signal immune cells to reduce activity; the IDO1 enzyme starts a separate route that breaks down tryptophan, an amino acid. Finding their components in a tumour does not prove immune suppression or drug benefit. An IDO1 blocker added to pembrolizumab did not improve melanoma outcomes in a phase 3 trial.
records.summary: The adenosine route works outside cells. CD39 (ENTPD1) and CD73 (NT5E) are enzymes that help generate adenosine from extracellular ATP and ADP, and adenosine then acts on cell-surface receptors, including the A2A receptor on T cells. The enzymes can sit on immune cells, cancer cells or other tissue cells, so the source has to be measured and not assumed. The IDO route works inside a producing cell: IDO1 starts the breakdown of tryptophan along the kynurenine pathway. IDO is not an adenosine receptor and does not degrade ATP, so the two routes should not be merged into one 'suppressive axis'.

notes: The mechanism evidence is mostly from mice and cell experiments. CD39 and CD73 distinguished regulatory T cells from other T cells, and regulatory T cells from Cd39-null mice had impaired suppression in vitro and failed to block allograft rejection in vivo (Deaglio et al., 2007). Deleting the A2A receptor in the host led to rejection of established immunogenic tumours in about 60 per cent of A2A-deficient mice, with none rejected in normal mice (Ohta et al., 2006). The same mouse study reported autoimmunity during melanoma rejection in the A2A-deficient mice and proposed that the receptor in T cells also helps prevent autoimmune tissue damage, so a pathway that restrains antitumour T cells may also protect normal tissue, and any assessment of an inhibitor has to weigh that trade-off. A subset of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in mouse tumour-draining lymph nodes expressed immunosuppressive levels of IDO and suppressed T-cell responses, and anergy was prevented by disrupting the IDO gene or by an IDO inhibitor (Munn et al., 2004). The same paper reported, as a separate observation in the human samples studied, that IDO-expressing cells in tumour-draining lymph nodes correlated with a worse clinical outcome; that is an association, and the authors noted the human cells' relationship to the mouse subset was still to be determined.

The layers of evidence are different and should be kept apart: a protein or RNA signal shows a component is present, a biochemical assay shows enzyme activity or metabolite, a functional experiment shows an immune effect, and a trial shows whether blocking it helps patients. A blood adenosine result is sensitive to handling: adenosine has a half-life of 1 to 2 seconds in human blood at 37 degrees Celsius, and in a sampling experiment recovery of labelled adenosine was 89 per cent with an inhibitor mix delivered at the catheter tip but 7 per cent when the mix was added only after the catheter (Shryock et al., 1990), and even a well-handled blood level does not locate the producing cells. No single expression cutoff for CD39, CD73 or IDO1 is validated in the sources cited here to choose an inhibitor, so a report should state the sample site, timing and units and not rely on one threshold. The clinical test of the IDO1 route was negative for that regimen: in ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252, 706 people with unresectable or metastatic melanoma not previously treated with a PD-1 or PD-L1 blocker received pembrolizumab with epacadostat or with placebo, and median progression-free survival was 4.7 against 4.9 months (hazard ratio 1.00, 95 per cent confidence interval 0.83 to 1.21), with overall survival hazard ratio 1.13 (0.86 to 1.49) (Long et al., 2019). The authors wrote that the usefulness of IDO1 inhibition to enhance anti-PD-1 therapy remains uncertain. That bounds one drug, one dose and one disease; it neither proves all IDO research futile nor validates another inhibitor or cancer. By the same logic, a tumour section that stains for both CD73 and IDO1 shows two measured proteins in the sampled cells: it does not show one dominant suppressive mechanism or the best inhibitor, because each route still needs its own activity and functional question.

records.tldr: An engineered cell can place a payload under the control of a naturally regulated gene. The resulting expression pattern still needs measurement in the actual cells and tissues.
records.summary: A CRISPR knock-in can connect an engineered cytokine payload to regulatory control at an endogenous gene locus. In preclinical work, NR4A2 and RGS16 control supported cytokine expression in specified CAR T-cell settings, with tumor and safety measurements in mouse models. This is distinct from adding synthetic response elements to a separate promoter. Neither the locus name nor an activation-responsive design proves tumor-only secretion, clinical safety or patient benefit.

Keep trigger recognition, payload transcription, secretion, tissue distribution and downstream activity separate. The IL-12 TIL clinical experience shows why inducible production alone cannot establish confinement or freedom from systemic toxicity. records.name: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS)
records.tldr: Cytokine release syndrome is systemic inflammation after immune activation, assessed through clinical findings and competing causes rather than a cytokine level alone.
records.summary:
Cytokine release syndrome can follow activation by engineered immune cells or T-cell-engaging treatments. Signals from several cell types can contribute to fever, hypotension, hypoxia and other organ effects. Infection or other conditions can produce similar findings or coexist with the syndrome.

The 2019 ASTCT consensus defines and grades CRS using attributed clinical findings, including fever at onset and the blood-pressure or oxygen support required. Its scale is a reporting framework, not a management algorithm. The 2026 ASTCT consensus expands the toxicity framework, but its detailed criteria were not accessible for this entry; the numerical grading below is explicitly the 2019 version. Product, disease, preparation, observation window and treated denominator must accompany any incidence estimate.

notes: How CRS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. The definition requires a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher that cannot be attributed to another cause. Severity is then the more severe of two findings, again not attributable to another cause. Grade 1 has neither. Grade 2 is low blood pressure that does not need vasopressors and/or oxygen by low-flow nasal cannula (up to 6 litres a minute) or blow-by. Grade 3 is one vasopressor, with or without vasopressin, and/or high-flow cannula, face mask, non-rebreather mask or Venturi mask. Grade 4 is multiple vasopressors, excluding vasopressin, and/or positive pressure such as CPAP, BiPAP or intubation. Once someone has had a fever-lowering or anti-cytokine treatment such as tocilizumab or steroids, fever is no longer needed to grade later severity: the grade then follows blood pressure and oxygen, and the person still counts as having CRS until the signs resolve. Organ toxicities linked to CRS are graded separately and do not change the CRS grade, and neurotoxicity during or after CRS is scored on the neurotoxicity scale, not added here. The 2026 ASTCT update (Perales et al.) convened experts to consider updating CRS, ICANS and haemophagocytic-lymphohistiocytosis-like grading, but only its abstract could be read, so whether it keeps, changes or relaxes any of these 2019 rules is not stated here; a report should say which version graded it.

Reading CRS without over-reading a cytokine level. CRS is a clinical syndrome, graded from attributed findings and not from a cytokine concentration. In a mouse model of CD19 CAR T-cell CRS, severity was mediated not by CAR T-cell-derived cytokines but by IL-6, IL-1 and nitric oxide from the recipient's macrophages, and IL-1 blockade abated it (Giavridis et al.); that supports a multicell amplification mechanism and does not show the same sources or shares in every human product. Infection and other conditions can cause or accompany the same findings, so the cause of a fever cannot be read from timing alone. A comparable report gives its grading version, observation window and treated denominator, with onset, maximum grade, interventions and resolution. Safety belongs to the product, disease, tumour burden and preparation, so experience with one blood-cancer product does not supply a solid-tumour product's rate, and no severe CRS in a small early study does not rule out uncommon events. CRS is a different problem from injury to healthy tissue that carries the target (on-target, off-tumour) and from neurotoxicity (ICANS). The treatment need not carry a cytokine payload to trigger endogenous inflammatory signalling. Tumour response does not establish acceptable inflammatory risk, and mild CRS does not establish lack of anticancer activity. Stopping a treatment input does not guarantee immediate removal of released signals or established injury. In a fictional early study, no severe CRS and a modest cytokine rise would not make every fever harmless CRS: attribution, clinical findings, a named grading framework, treated denominator and observation window are still needed.

Use the named consensus version when classifying immune-effector-cell toxicities. The 2026 ASTCT abstract describes updates to CRS, ICANS and IEC-HS and consensus work on haematotoxicity, non-ICANS neurologic events such as parkinsonism or cranial-nerve palsies, enterocolitis, tumour-inflammation-associated neurotoxicity and on-target off-tumour toxicity. It covers immune-effector-cell and T-cell-engager therapy. These category names do not diagnose an event from timing alone or supply the detailed grading criteria; clinical assessment still has to distinguish other causes. The absence of an added cytokine payload does not rule out inflammatory syndromes.

Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says almost everyone treated with engineered T-cell therapy has some level of cytokine release syndrome, that it most commonly develops within 10 days of the infusion, and that most cases are mild and easily treated. The signs it lists are fever and chills, a rapid heart rate, low blood pressure, low oxygen, headache, and feeling or being sick. Severe cases are treated with oxygen, fluids, steroids and tocilizumab, and usually improve within a few days. Around one person in five who has this treatment needs intensive care.

records.name: ICANS (neurotoxicity)
records.tldr: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome can affect language, attention, awareness or other brain functions; a cognitive score is one part of clinical assessment.
records.summary:
Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, or ICANS, is a neurologic syndrome associated with immune-effector-cell therapy. Changes in language, attention, handwriting or awareness and more severe findings such as seizures need assessment against baseline and alternative explanations. An immune-marker plot does not establish the syndrome.

The 2019 ASTCT adult framework combines the immune effector cell-associated encephalopathy (ICE) score with consciousness, seizures, motor findings and raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema. Children require age-appropriate assessment. The 2026 consensus also addresses non-ICANS neurologic toxicities; its detailed tables were not accessible for this entry. Neurologic events and recovery need their own record rather than being inferred from resolution of CRS.

notes: How ICANS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. For adults, the grade is the most severe of five findings, none attributable to another cause. The 10-point ICE screen of orientation, naming, command-following, writing and attention scores 7 to 9 for grade 1, 3 to 6 for grade 2, 0 to 2 for grade 3, and 0 because the person is unarousable and cannot be tested for grade 4; an ICE of 0 in someone who is awake with global aphasia can still be grade 3. Level of consciousness counts only if no other cause such as a sedating medicine explains it: awakens spontaneously, awakens to voice, only to touch, or unarousable or requiring vigorous or repeated tactile stimulation. Any seizure that resolves rapidly, or EEG-only seizures that resolve with treatment, is grade 3, and prolonged (over 5 minutes) or repeated seizures without return to baseline are grade 4. Deep focal motor weakness is grade 4, while tremor and myoclonus may be graded on CTCAE but do not change the ICANS grade. Focal oedema on imaging is grade 3; diffuse oedema, posturing, cranial nerve VI palsy, papilloedema or Cushing's triad is grade 4; intracranial haemorrhage is excluded from ICANS grading. So ICE is a screen for encephalopathy and one input, not the whole examination: a person with an ICE of 3 who has a generalised seizure is grade 3, and headache alone is not a useful marker. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract adds categories such as non-ICANS neurological toxicities (parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsies, polyneuropathies) and tumour inflammation-associated neurotoxicity; their criteria, and any change to how ICE is used, were not readable here.

What is known about mechanism, timing and attribution. In 133 adults given CD19 CAR T cells, Gust et al. found that those with severe neurotoxicity had endothelial activation (disseminated intravascular coagulation, capillary leak) and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, and that the permeable barrier failed to protect the cerebrospinal fluid from high systemic cytokine concentrations including interferon-gamma. Higher risk went with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, high marrow CD19-positive burden, high CAR T-cell dose, CRS and pre-existing neurological disease, and markers of endothelial activation before lymphodepletion were higher in people who later had grade 4 or worse neurotoxicity. That is an association in one product class and population, not a complete mechanism for every treatment. ICANS can accompany CRS or follow its own timetable, and neurotoxicity after CRS is scored separately, so recovery of blood pressure and oxygen does not show neurological recovery. If a person is confused while taking a sedating medicine and the ICE score falls, the grading rule requires that sedation be excluded, so the fall calls for clinical assessment, neither ignored nor diagnosed from the score alone. Clinical assessment also considers infection, metabolic disturbances, medicines and pre-existing neurologic disease. A safety report should retain onset, severity, attributed cause, interventions, duration, recovery and how many people were adequately observed. Separate fictional CRS and neurologic timelines can end at different times; they do not specify a typical order or duration. Stopping an engineered input does not guarantee immediate reversal of established neurologic injury.

Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says around one person in four treated with engineered T-cell therapy develops neurotoxicity, that it generally appears within 28 days of the infusion and often within a few days, and that symptoms are usually mild and resolve in a week or two. The signs it lists are confusion, speech problems, difficulty writing, headache and dizziness, shaking or tremor, and difficulty moving. Seizures and brain swelling are the serious forms. Someone who develops it is advised not to drive for 8 weeks from the onset of symptoms, and the requirement to have another adult present for the four weeks after infusion exists because the person affected is often the last to notice.

records.name: Mesothelin-targeting T cell receptor fusion construct cell therapy in refractory solid tumors: phase 1/2 trial interim results
records.tldr: Published report from the Phase 1 trial registered as NCT03907852, in Nature Medicine (2023), chosen as the most cited paper whose own text cites the registry id.
records.summary:
The T cell receptor fusion construct (TRuC) gavocabtagene autoleucel (gavo-cel) consists of single-domain anti-mesothelin antibody that integrates into the endogenous T cell receptor (TCR) and engages the signaling capacity of the entire TCR upon mesothelin binding. Here we describe phase 1 results from an ongoing phase1/2 trial of gavo-cel in patients with treatment-refractory mesothelin-expressing solid tumors. The primary objectives were to evaluate safety and determine the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). Secondary objectives included efficacy. Thirty-two patients received gavo-cel at increasing doses either as a single agent (n = 3) or after lymphodepletion (LD, n = 29). Dose-limiting toxicities of grade 3 pneumonitis and grade 5 bronchioalveolar hemorrhage were noted. The RP2D was determined as 1 × 10 8 cells per m 2 after LD. Grade 3 or higher pneumonitis was seen in 16% of all patients and in none at the RP2D; grade 3 or higher cytokine release syndrome occurred in 25% of all patients and in 15% at the RP2D. In 30 evaluable patients, the overall response rate and disease control rate were 20% (13% confirmed) and 77%, respectively, and the 6-month overall survival rate was 70%. Gavo-cel warrants further study in patients with mesothelin-expressing cancers given its encouraging anti-tumor activity, but it may have a narrow therapeutic window. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03907852.

Indexed on Europe PMC as PubMed record 37501016 (DOI 10.1038/s41591-023-02452-y). Its abstract cites the registry id NCT03907852, which is how it was matched to this trial; no figure has been checked by an editor.

notes: This historical single-arm phase-I dose-escalation report, within a phase-I/II programme, used a 9 September 2022 cutoff. Gavo-cel comprised autologous T cells engineered ex vivo with an antibody-CD3-epsilon fusion recognising surface mesothelin without a conventional peptide-HLA requirement. The treated cancers were mesothelioma, ovarian cancer and cholangiocarcinoma. Forty-eight people underwent apheresis intending phase-I infusion, 32 were treated and 30 were response-evaluable. Two grade-5 adverse events occurred before post-infusion imaging. Blinded independent central review found six responses, four confirmed partial responses: 6/30 is 20 per cent, 6/48 is 12.5 per cent and 4/30 is about 13.3 per cent, reported as 13 per cent. Each fraction needs its analysis population, reviewer, rule and confirmation status. Missing scans do not settle safety or causal attribution, and this study does not estimate comparative benefit in another cancer. Response confirmation, response duration, survival and quality of life are different outcomes. The historical cutoff and a source-check date do not establish current recruitment, approval, availability or personal eligibility.

Among the 32 treated participants, 25 had cytokine release syndrome: 17 grade 1 or 2, six grade 3 and two grade 4. One person had brief, self-limited ICANS. The report used the 2019 ASTCT framework for those syndromes and CTCAE version 5 for other adverse events. Tocilizumab was given to 17 participants with CRS, including 11 also given corticosteroids; eight did not require anti-cytokine treatment. Everyone infused had at least 12 weeks of safety follow-up. Median CRS onset was three days (range zero to nine), and median duration was six days (range one to 55). These are observations under the report’s rules, not a bedside treatment algorithm, an explanation of each clinician’s decision or a randomised estimate that an intervention caused recovery.

records.name: TIL therapy
records.tldr: TIL therapy expands lymphocytes collected from a tumor and returns a prepared cell product. Tissue origin, culture yield and useful tumor recognition are different claims.
records.summary:
Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy starts with cells collected from tumor tissue, commonly using their existing T-cell receptors. Infiltration does not prove that every cell recognizes the cancer. Culture and selection can change which clones become abundant; final viable-cell yield, recognition breadth and useful function need their own evidence. Manufacturing, conditioning, cytokine support and follow-up form a complete regimen with separate contributions and harms.

Lifileucel (Amtagvi) received accelerated FDA approval in 2024 for specified previously treated unresectable or metastatic melanoma. Its label defines the prior-treatment conditions and regimen. TILVANCE-301 is a phase 3 advanced-melanoma study of a lifileucel regimen with pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab. Neither a registry design nor clinical evidence from one TIL process establishes benefit for every tumor or manufacturing method.
